newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: U.S. embassy, residence phones cut in Abidjan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. embassy, residence phones cut in Abidjan.

text.p: Telephones at the U.S. embassy in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, and in homes of its diplomats have been cut since the start of the week because of a problem over bills, U.S. diplomats and Ivorian officials said on Friday.
Agencies of the U.S. government, including the aid arm USAID, the American Cultural Centre, U.S. Commercial Services and the Voice of America are all without phones, they said.

"It is part of a general programme to recover our arrears," an official of Ivorian telephone monopoly CI-TELCOM told Reuters. CI-TELCOM wanted to tighten its credit control ahead of its privatisation due before year's end and had given notice of its current drive in newspaper advertisements a month ago.
The home telephone of Ambassador Lannon Walker was still working but the embassy declined official comment.

Telephone bills of the American embassy and U.S. agencies are paid centrally. A diplomat, who asked not to be identified, said a new CI-TELCOM computer which automatically disconnects accounts in arrears may be responsible.
Sources close to the embassy said the embassy accounts were only a day late. CI-TELCOM had no immediate comment on this.
U.S. embassy officials, privately, discounted any idea that Americans were being targeted. One diplomat said he knew of several European-owned businesses that had been disconnected in the past week.
Frustrated U.S. government staff sat stone-faced at their desks on Friday morning, cut off from the rest of Abidjan and the world, and worst of all, from their electronic mail.
Asked how business was being conducted, an official at one agency said: "With difficulty."
